strengths: The paper presents a clear and relevant formulation of single-image motion forecasting as conditional generation of quasi-dense trajectory grids. The latent flow-matching architecture is technically coherent and provides useful inductive biases for object permanence, temporal coherence, and scene-wide interactions.

The empirical scope is unusually broad: experiments cover Kubric, LIBERO, Physics101, and Physion, with comparisons against trajectory regressors, a diffusion-based trajectory generator, motion-generation methods, and several large video generators.

The Kubric evaluation considers complementary aspects of performance, including conditional distribution matching, best-of-K accuracy, rigidity, out-of-distribution objects, computational cost, and human preference. The matched-architecture output-modality experiment provides meaningful evidence that predicting trajectories can be more effective and efficient than predicting RGB.

The appendix contains substantial implementation detail, resource estimates, model configurations, baseline protocols, and useful ablations of latent-space modeling, model scale, and pseudo-ground-truth tracks. The method is also substantially faster and smaller than the evaluated video generators.
The paper is clearly motivated and generally well written, and it explicitly discusses limitations and potential misuse in surveillance or behavioral prediction.
weaknesses: The paper does not cleanly isolate two central causal claims. The comparisons with ATM and Tra-MoE simultaneously change stochastic versus deterministic prediction, architecture, model capacity, and sparse versus dense trajectories. There is no controlled regression-versus-generation or sparse-versus-grid ablation, so the claimed reasons for the gains are not established.

The strongest trajectory baseline, Track2Act, is substantially modified beyond its original setting: its goal frame is removed, its horizon is tripled, and its output is expanded from at most 400 points to 1,024. Poor performance under this altered configuration is not necessarily representative of the published method, and stronger contemporary dense motion/flow forecasting baselines are limited.

Some reported Kubric results appear internally inconsistent. For nominally the same in-distribution evaluation, the proposed base model has FVMD/FVMD(S) values of 12,221/14,950 in Table 12 but 5,713.7/8,309.7 in Table 11; the large model changes from 13,745/17,838 to 6,470.3/9,293.0. The protocol does not explain these large differences, weakening confidence in the quantitative comparisons and reproducibility.

Metric validation is incomplete. FVMD is acknowledged to be coarse, the proposed scene-wise version receives only a small sanity check, and LRTL can reward static predictions and relies on simulator-provided object masks. Occlusion handling and the construction and aggregation of best-of-K matches are not specified sufficiently precisely.

The user study is small—20 participants and 16 scenes—and reports no confidence intervals, statistical tests, participant-level aggregation, or treatment of repeated observations. Consequently, the claim that the ELO score is 'significantly' higher is unsupported.

Evidence on real data is comparatively weak. Physics101 has only one target future and one generated sample, the overall improvement over WAN is modest (28.62 versus 30.08 MSE) with losses in two of five scenarios, and synthetic-to-real Physion generalization is qualitative. No downstream control or decision-making evaluation demonstrates that the predicted distributions are practically useful.

Despite extensive hyperparameter reporting, the paper does not state that code, trained models, generated evaluation splits, or metric implementations will be released. Reproduction would also require substantial compute, while random-seed variability and error bars are absent from the main quantitative experiments.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and intrinsically uncertain problem: forecasting scene-wide motion from a single image.
Representing motion as a dense trajectory grid is intuitive, computationally attractive, and potentially useful for robotics and physical prediction.
The architecture is clearly presented, and the experiments cover several datasets, trajectory and video baselines, synthetic-to-real transfer, design ablations, inference cost, and a user study.
The appendix provides substantial implementation and compute details, and the paper appropriately discusses limitations and potential misuse.
weaknesses: The central causal claim—that video generators fail because of the overhead of RGB generation—is not established. Changing output modality also changes the VAE, representation, temporal structure, reconstruction pipeline, and tracking stage. Similar latent dimensionality and good RGB reconstruction scores do not isolate pixel-generation overhead; motion should at least be measured after reconstructing ground-truth videos through each RGB VAE.

The comparisons do not cleanly support the claimed reasons for improvement. There is no controlled ablation separating stochastic generation from regression, dense grids from selected points, or DINO patch conditioning from global image conditioning. The fact that the proposed model already wins with one sample on LIBERO suggests architectural and capacity differences, not demonstrated benefits from modeling uncertainty.

Baseline fairness is questionable. Track2Act is substantially modified by removing goal conditioning, tripling its horizon, and increasing its point count beyond its original regime while retaining default hyperparameters. Video generators are fine-tuned for equal wall-clock duration rather than to convergence or with matched optimization budgets, which disadvantages much larger models.

Several apparently corresponding Kubric results are inconsistent without explanation. For example, Ours (L) has FVMD 13,745 in Tables 3 and 12 but 6,470 in Table 11; its LRTL differs between Tables 3 and 12 despite otherwise identical values; and the in-distribution track result in Table 6 matches the result labeled out-of-distribution in Table 4. These discrepancies substantially undermine confidence in the evaluation.

The distributional evaluation is under-specified and statistically weak. Best-of-K matching is not defined precisely, FVMD(S) is estimated from only 64 futures for each of 16 scenes, and there are no confidence intervals, repeated training seeds, significance tests, calibration measurements, or quality-diversity curves. Best-of-K inherently rewards additional samples and is not directly comparable with deterministic baselines.

LRTL is a limited proxy for physical plausibility: static or collapsed predictions can score well, and low-rank 2D tracks do not verify collision behavior, object permanence, gravity, or other physical laws. The paper acknowledges one degeneracy but still uses the metric to make broad physical-consistency claims.

The real-world evidence is not convincing. On Physics101, the overall improvement over WAN is small, the method loses in two of five scenarios, evaluation uses a single sample and CoTracker pseudo-ground truth, and no uncertainty estimates are given. Synthetic-to-real generalization is supported only by a few qualitative examples.

The video comparison compounds generation errors with tracking errors. CoTracker is validated on ground-truth Kubric videos, not on videos containing generator-specific appearance artifacts, so the experiment cannot distinguish incorrect physical motion from failures of the video-to-track measurement pipeline.
The user study is small and lacks confidence intervals or an appropriate participant-aware statistical analysis, despite claiming a significant ELO advantage.

Overall, the method is largely a direct combination of established components—trajectory grids, a conditional VAE, rectified flow, DINO features, and a Latte-style transformer. This could still be useful engineering, but the novelty and evidence are insufficient for the paper's broad explanatory claims and for acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and relevant formulation of single-image motion forecasting as conditional generation of quasi-dense point-trajectory grids. Directly modeling motion is a sensible alternative to generating RGB video and then recovering motion with a tracker.

The empirical scope is unusually broad: experiments cover Kubric, LIBERO, Physics101, and Physion, with comparisons to regression-based trajectory predictors, a generative trajectory method, and several large video generators.

The Kubric results are compelling overall. The proposed method substantially improves distributional, best-of-K, and rigidity metrics, including on an out-of-distribution object split. The fixed-architecture modality study in Table 6 provides useful evidence that trajectory generation can be more effective than RGB generation for this task.

The paper includes meaningful analyses beyond headline comparisons, including latent-space and model-scale ablations, training with estimated rather than ground-truth tracks, tracker validation, computational-cost measurements, a user study, and explicit physical-consistency evaluation.
The method and training setup are described clearly, with extensive architectural, hyperparameter, hardware, and evaluation details. Ethical risks and limitations are also acknowledged.
weaknesses: Several causal claims are stronger than the experiments support. The claimed benefits of stochastic generation and dense scene-wide reasoning are not isolated using controlled ablations with the same architecture. Comparisons against ATM and Tra-MoE change the architecture, representation, number of predicted points, and objective simultaneously.

The Track2Act comparison substantially modifies that baseline by removing goal conditioning, tripling its prediction horizon, and increasing its output from at most 400 points to 1,024. Although these changes align the task, they may place Track2Act far outside its validated regime, weakening conclusions about generative trajectory baselines.

The assertion that video generators fail specifically because of RGB-generation overhead remains suggestive rather than conclusive. Table 6 controls the backbone and uses roughly comparable latent shapes, but the modalities still employ different autoencoders, channel dimensions, target complexity, and potentially different effective capacities. Only RGB reconstruction quality is reported; comparable trajectory-autoencoder reconstruction and compute-controlled analyses are missing.

The real-world evidence is relatively weak. On Physics101, evaluation uses a single CoTracker-derived pseudo-ground truth and one sample per model; the overall improvement over WAN is modest, and the method loses in two of five scenarios. Physion-to-real generalization is supported primarily by a small qualitative demonstration.

There are unexplained numerical inconsistencies across tables. For example, the Kubric FVMD values for Ours (L) in Tables 3 and 4 differ dramatically from those reported for the same named model and splits in Table 11. Table 6 also reports yet another configuration without clearly identifying it in the table. These discrepancies should be reconciled before publication.

The proposed metrics have limitations that are only partially addressed. Best-of-K rewards sample count and coverage, LRTL can favor static predictions, and FVMD relies on coarse handcrafted motion statistics. Ground-truth calibration is provided for only some metrics, and no uncertainty estimates or repeated-training variation are reported.

The user study is small and lacks confidence intervals, significance tests, participant details, and agreement analysis, despite the text describing the ELO difference as significant. Code and processed benchmark release plans are also unclear, limiting practical reproducibility despite the strong implementation appendix.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and practically useful formulation of uncertain single-image motion forecasting as conditional generation of quasi-dense point-trajectory grids.
The latent flow-matching architecture is technically plausible and combines scene-wide DINO conditioning, spatiotemporal attention, and an image-conditioned trajectory VAE in a coherent design.

The empirical scope is unusually broad: comparisons include trajectory regressors, trajectory generators, pretrained and fine-tuned video generators, synthetic and real-world datasets, out-of-distribution shapes, and a controlled output-modality study.

The authors evaluate complementary aspects of performance, including distributional similarity, best-of-K accuracy, rigidity, human preference, inference cost, and point-tracker reliability. Most comparisons consistently favor the proposed representation.

The appendix provides substantial architecture, hyperparameter, resource, baseline-protocol, ablation, ethics, and limitations information. The method is also substantially faster and smaller than the evaluated video generators.
weaknesses: The main conceptual ingredients—latent flow matching, a trajectory VAE, factorized video-transformer blocks, and dense grid prediction—are largely adaptations of established techniques. The novelty is therefore primarily in the formulation and empirical study rather than a major methodological advance.

The central causal claim that RGB-generation overhead is responsible for inferior motion modeling is stronger than the evidence. Even the controlled modality comparison uses different VAEs and latent channel counts, while the large video baselines differ in pretraining, architecture, resolution, temporal compression, capacity, and fine-tuning behavior.

The principal Kubric evaluation contains only 16 distinct initial scenes per split, with 64 velocity rollouts per scene. Thus, the large stated sample count overstates the number of independent visual conditions, and no confidence intervals or variability across training runs are reported.

Several reported results appear internally inconsistent without explanation. For example, the same Kubric models have markedly different FVMD/LRTL values across Tables 3, 13, 14, and 17; even Ours (L) has LRTL 14.1 in Table 3 versus 14.6 in Table 14. Table 17 additionally selects the best checkpoint separately for each metric, which can produce an optimistic, non-realizable aggregate.

The evaluation metrics have important limitations. Image-wise FVMD is estimated from very small per-scene sample sets, its validation is minimal, LRTL rewards static motion, and the exact matching procedure underlying Best-of-K is insufficiently specified. Statistical significance is absent throughout.

Baseline fairness is not fully convincing. Track2Act is substantially altered by removing goal conditioning and extending both its horizon and point count, while large video generators are fine-tuned for the same wall-clock duration as a much smaller model rather than being tuned to convergence or equalized by optimization budget.

The real-world evidence is weaker than the presentation suggests: Physics101 improves only modestly overall and loses on two of five scenarios; Cityscapes and Physics101 rely on a single CoTracker-derived target and MSE, which cannot assess the intended multimodal distribution; Physion-to-real generalization is qualitative and very small scale.

The user study is underpowered and incompletely analyzed: only 20 participants and 16 scenes are used, with no confidence intervals, significance tests, participant information, or agreement analysis. A 52% first-place rate does not by itself establish a robust preference.

Reproducibility remains limited despite detailed hyperparameters: no code or trained-model release is specified, some dataset construction and split details are missing, and full reproduction is estimated to require substantial compute.

The paper includes useful studies of the VAE latent space, model scale, trajectory density, estimated rather than ground-truth tracks, RGB-versus-trajectory generation, and joint RGB/trajectory generation.

weaknesses: The central causal claims are not cleanly isolated. Comparisons with regression systems simultaneously change stochasticity, trajectory density, architecture, capacity, image encoding, and conditioning. A matched deterministic version of the proposed architecture and controlled sparse-versus-dense comparisons are needed to establish that generation and scene-wide reasoning cause the gains.

Several baselines are questionable controls. Track2Act is materially altered by removing goal conditioning, tripling its horizon, and increasing its output from at most 400 points to 1,024 while retaining default hyperparameters. ATM and Tra-MoE target goal-conditioned robotic motion rather than general physical forecasting. Fine-tuning video generators for the same wall-clock duration does not establish comparable optimization or convergence.

The physical evaluation is too weak for the paper's claims. LRTL is only a low-rank proxy and is minimized by static predictions; it does not test collisions, penetration, contact, gravity, conservation, or object permanence. Best-of-K is oracle-based and rewards sample count or diffuse predictions, while FVMD relies on coarse marginal histogram features. Table 24's two-point sanity check is insufficient metric validation.

The headline Kubric evaluation contains only 16 scene configurations per split, with 64 velocity rollouts each, and the OOD split changes object primitives rather than dynamics, materials, or scene composition. Thus, the effective diversity of initial visual conditions is small and the claimed physical generalization is narrow.

The real-world evidence does not convincingly validate multimodal forecasting. Physics101 and Cityscapes provide only one pseudo-ground-truth future per image and are scored by MSE; Physics101 improves only slightly overall and loses on two of five scenarios. Cityscapes uses CoTracker-generated targets for training/evaluation and CoTracker again to extract motion from video baselines, introducing representation and tracker confounds.

Important numerical and protocol inconsistencies reduce confidence. The same Ours-L Kubric result has LRTL 14.1 in Table 3 and 14.6 in Table 14; Table 13 reports substantially different FVMD and LRTL values for apparently the same Kubric splits without explaining the changed protocol; and Table 17 uses very different metric scales. Uncertainty intervals and repeated-run variation are absent throughout.

The user study is small, lacks confidence intervals or significance testing despite claiming a significantly higher ELO, and appears to select displayed outputs according to Best-of-K, potentially introducing oracle selection bias.

The methodological novelty is moderate: latent flow matching, a trajectory VAE, factorized spatiotemporal attention, and dense point grids are mostly established components. Given the confounded comparisons and limited validation of physical plausibility, the evidence is not yet strong enough to support the broad conclusion that direct trajectory modeling is generally superior to video-based world modeling.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and useful formulation of single-image motion forecasting as conditional generation of quasi-dense point trajectories. Directly representing motion provides sensible inductive biases for temporal coherence and object permanence while avoiding the computational burden of pixel synthesis.

The empirical scope is unusually broad: experiments cover Kubric, LIBERO, Physics101, Cityscapes, and Physion, with comparisons against regression-based trajectory predictors, a generative trajectory method, and several pretrained or fine-tuned video generators.

Results are consistently favorable on the principal Kubric benchmarks. The proposed method improves distributional, best-of-K, and rigidity metrics while being substantially smaller and faster than video-generation baselines. The controlled modality experiment and joint RGB-plus-trajectory experiment provide particularly useful evidence for the value of explicit motion representations.

The paper includes meaningful design studies on latent versus raw trajectory generation, model scale, trajectory density, pseudo-labeled tracks, and multi-frame conditioning. The collapse observed without the VAE offers a plausible empirical justification for latent generation.

Implementation details, architectures, hyperparameters, computational costs, tracker accuracy, limitations, and ethical considerations are documented relatively thoroughly. The presentation is generally clear and the qualitative visualizations complement the quantitative evaluation.
weaknesses: The strongest causal claim—that video generators fail because of the overhead of RGB generation—is not fully isolated. The modality comparison also changes the VAE, latent channel count and temporal compression, and the trajectory autoencoder is explicitly conditioned on the input image. Equal training time and a shared denoiser do not eliminate these representation and optimization confounders.

The physical-plausibility evidence remains limited. LRTL is only a low-rank rigidity proxy, can reward static predictions, and does not directly measure collision validity, gravity, penetration, conservation laws, or object permanence. The paper acknowledges one failure mode but does not provide stronger physics-specific tests.

Several evaluation choices weaken statistical confidence. Results appear to come from single training runs without confidence intervals; the small user study has only 20 participants and 16 scenes; and the density ablation reports the best metric among three late checkpoints, which can introduce selection bias. Statistical significance is asserted without a reported test.

Real-world evidence is less compelling than the synthetic results. Physics101 has only one pseudo-ground-truth future and shows a small overall gain over WAN while losing in two of five scenarios; Physion-to-real generalization is qualitative; and Cityscapes evaluation relies on CoTracker pseudo-labels and single-future MSE, which cannot establish calibrated multimodal forecasting.

Reproducibility and reporting have gaps despite extensive hyperparameter tables: the Kubric training-set size and generation configuration are not clearly specified, code and trained-model availability are not stated, and markedly different FVMD/LRTL scales across Tables 3, 6, 13, 14, and 17 are insufficiently explained. The baselines also require substantial task-specific modifications, making some comparisons less definitive than comparisons to purpose-built dense generative trajectory models would be.
